question: How does Marcus advise preparing for the difficult people you'll meet each day?
answer: Begin the morning by telling yourself you'll meet the busybody, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious and unsocial. They act from ignorance of good and evil; they're your kin, sharing the same reason, so they can't injure you and you shouldn't be angry with them or hate them. We're made for cooperation, like feet, hands and eyelids. (Book II.1)

question: What are the nine rules for dealing with someone who has offended you?
answer: 1) We're made for one another. 2) Consider what they're like and what opinions compel them. 3) If they do wrong, it's involuntary and from ignorance. 4) You also do wrong and have the disposition to. 5) You can't be sure they're doing wrong at all. 6) Life is a moment; we'll soon be dead. 7) Their acts don't disturb us, our opinions do. 8) Anger brings more pain than the act. 9) A genuine good disposition is invincible: correct them gently, affectionately, without reproach, ideally in private. A tenth gift: expecting bad men not to do wrong is madness. (Book XI.18)

question: Where does Marcus say our disturbances come from?
answer: Not from things, which don't touch the soul and remain outside it, but only from the opinion within us. 'The universe is transformation: life is opinion.' (Book IV.3)

question: What reasons does Marcus give for not being tormented by the desire for fame?
answer: Everything is soon forgotten; infinite time lies on either side of the present; applause is empty; those who praise are changeable and lack judgement; the earth is a point, and few in its small corner will praise you. (Book IV.3)

question: What warning does Marcus give himself about becoming emperor?
answer: 'Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar, that thou art not dyed with this dye; for such things happen.' Keep yourself simple, good, pure, serious, free from affectation, just, kind and affectionate. (Book VI.30)

question: What does Marcus say is worth valuing, if not fame?
answer: Not applause: the praise of the many is 'a clapping of tongues'. What's worth valuing is directing and restraining yourself according to your own constitution. Valuing externals makes you unfree, envious, jealous and suspicious of those who might take them away. (Book VI.16)

question: Where does Marcus say a person can truly retreat?
answer: Into his own soul. People seek country houses, seashores and mountains, but you can retire into yourself whenever you choose, and nowhere is quieter or freer from trouble. (Book IV.3)

question: What two rules should a person always keep ready?
answer: 1) Do only what reason, the ruling and legislating faculty, suggests for the use of men. 2) Change your opinion if someone sets you right, but only from persuasion of what is just or of common advantage, not because it's pleasant or brings reputation. (Book IV.12)

question: Who introduced Marcus to the discourses of Epictetus?
answer: Rusticus, who shared them from his own collection. (Book I.7)

question: What virtues did Marcus observe in his adoptive father?
answer: Mildness of temper, firm resolution after deliberation, no vainglory about honours, love of labour and perseverance, readiness to hear proposals for the common good, giving each person their due, checking applause and flattery, simplicity, and patience under blame. (Book I.16)

question: Where were Books I and II written?
answer: Book I 'among the Quadi at the Granua'; Book II 'in Carnuntum'.

question: What does Marcus tell himself when he doesn't want to get out of bed?
answer: 'I am rising to the work of a human being.' Was he made to lie in the bedclothes and keep warm? Plants, birds, ants, spiders and bees do their work; rest is necessary, but nature sets limits to it. (Book V.1)

question: What does Marcus call the best way to take revenge?
answer: Not to become like the wrongdoer. (Book VI.6)

question: How does Marcus strip impressive things of their show?
answer: By seeing them as they are: fine food is the dead body of a fish, bird or pig; Falernian wine is grape juice; a purple robe is sheep's wool dyed with shellfish blood. Do the same with everything that seems worth admiring. (Book VI.13)

question: Should you apply principles like a gladiator or a pancratiast, and why?
answer: Like a pancratiast: the gladiator can drop his sword and be killed, but the pancratiast always has his hands and only needs to use them. (Book XII.9)

question: How should you do every act of your life?
answer: As if it were the last, setting aside carelessness, passionate aversion to reason, hypocrisy, self-love and discontent with your lot. (Book II.5)

question: What does Marcus find strange about how people value opinions of themselves?
answer: Everyone loves himself more than all others, yet values his own opinion of himself less than others' opinion of him. (Book XII.4)

question: What four aberrations of the ruling faculty should you guard against?
answer: Thoughts that aren't necessary; thoughts that destroy social union; saying what doesn't come from your real thoughts; and reproaching yourself, which shows the divine part yielding to the body. (Book XI.19)

question: What does Marcus say about the Christians?
answer: Their only mention in the text: readiness to die should come from a man's own judgement, considerately and with dignity, 'not from mere obstinacy, as with the Christians'. (Book XI.3)

question: What does Marcus say about worrying about the future?
answer: 'Let not future things disturb thee', since you'll meet them with the same reason you use now (VII.8). Don't think of your whole life at once; ask what in this moment is intolerable. Neither future nor past pains you, only the present (VIII.36).

question: How does Marcus compare death to the end of a play?
answer: Like an actor dismissed from the stage by the praetor who hired him. Objecting 'I've played only three of the five acts' is answered: in life, three acts are the whole drama, and its end is set by the one who composed it. Depart content. (Book XII.36)

question: Someone cut me off in traffic and I was furious. What would Marcus say?
answer: The book doesn't discuss traffic, but anger at an offender is a core topic: the nine rules (they act from ignorance, you err too, anger hurts more than the act, correct gently); anger is weakness and gentleness is strength; expecting bad men not to do wrong is madness; and to be vexed at those who hinder you is a weakness. (XI.9, XI.18)

question: My friend is getting famous and it's going to his head. What lesson would he take from the book?
answer: Fame is empty and soon forgotten (IV.3); praise is 'a clapping of tongues', and valuing it makes you unfree and envious (VI.16); and Marcus's own warning: 'Take care that thou art not made into a Caesar… dyed with this dye' (VI.30).

question: I've been job hunting for months and I'm anxious. What would Marcus think?
answer: Don't think of the whole of your life at once; ask what in this moment is intolerable; only the present can pain you (VIII.36). Future things shouldn't disturb you, since you'll meet them with the same reason (VII.8). The anxiety comes from opinion, not the events (IV.3).

question: Who gave Marcus the teachings that introduced him to his main Stoic influence?
answer: Rusticus, who shared the discourses of Epictetus from his own collection. (Book I.7)

question: What's the best way to get back at someone who wronged me?
answer: Not to become like the wrongdoer. (Book VI.6)

question: How should I start a day when I know I'll deal with annoying people?
answer: Expect them in advance: the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant. Remember they act from ignorance and are your kin, so they can't harm you and you shouldn't hate them. (Book II.1)

question: I struggle to get out of bed in the morning. Does Marcus say anything about that?
answer: Yes: 'I am rising to the work of a human being.' He wasn't made to lie warm in bed; plants and animals do their work, and nature limits rest. (Book V.1)

question: I need a break, but I can't travel. Where can I find peace?
answer: In yourself: people seek country houses, seashores and mountains, but you can retreat into your own soul whenever you choose. (Book IV.3)

question: What does Marcus say about the Antonine Plague?
answer: Not covered. He never discusses the plague; IX.2 uses 'pestilence' only as a metaphor for a corrupted mind (p.79).

question: What does Marcus say about Seneca?
answer: Nothing: Marcus never mentions Seneca. The name appears only in the translator's endnotes.

question: What did Marcus think of his son Commodus?
answer: Not covered. Commodus is never named; Book I only thanks the gods for his children and their good teachers.

question: What does Marcus say about Jesus?
answer: Nothing: the name appears only in a translator's endnote. Marcus mentions the Christians once (XI.3), not Jesus.
